passage:
The client wanted the revised floor plans by six, and the office generator kept tripping in the heat. Madhuri had drawn the staircase three ways already. Each time, a message from Pankaj popped up: 'Send me what you have.' 'Why that width?' 'Wait, let me look first.'
By two o'clock she noticed she had stopped choosing anything. She sent even the door swings to him and sat staring at the frozen screen, waiting.
When the power came back, she walked to his desk. 'Pankaj, I know the deadline's tight. But when every step goes past you, I stop trusting my own eye, and we lose time. Can we check in at three and at five, and I decide in between?'
He rubbed his neck. 'Fair. Three and five.'
She finished the staircase by half past four.

qa.q: What check-in times did Madhuri suggest?
qa.a: Three and five, with Madhuri deciding in between.

qa.q: What does Madhuri sending even the door swings to Pankaj suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt distrusted and had lost faith in her own judgment, so she waited for approval instead of deciding.

qa.q: What turning point let Madhuri finish the staircase before the deadline?
qa.a: Walking to Pankaj's desk and calmly naming how the constant checking slowed her down, then agreeing on two check-ins, gave her room to decide again.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have seen his frequent messages before Madhuri spoke up?
qa.a: Pankaj may have seen them as protecting a tight deadline rather than as distrust, and his quick 'Fair' suggests he had not noticed their cost.

grounding: Shows a colleague under constant checking losing trust in her own judgment, then calmly naming the effect and agreeing on set check-in points.

passage:
Parul had rewritten Gurpreet's caption again, the fourth time that week. The bakery's page was his job, but lately he typed a post, sent it to her and waited. Yesterday a customer's question about eggless cakes sat unanswered for three hours because he didn't want to reply without her okay.
On Friday, with the ovens cooling and the shutter half down on the busy market lane, he pulled a stool up to her counter.
'Parul, when every post comes back changed, I start feeling you don't trust me with it. And I've stopped deciding, even small things.'
She wiped flour off her hands slowly. 'I didn't know it felt like that.'
They agreed: she would look over the weekly plan on Mondays, and he would handle daily replies alone. By Wednesday he had answered forty messages without asking once.

qa.q: Why did the customer's question about eggless cakes sit unanswered for three hours?
qa.a: Because Gurpreet didn't want to reply without Parul's okay.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel about Parul rewriting his captions?
qa.a: He felt she didn't trust him with the page, and it made him stop deciding even small things.

qa.q: What choice did Gurpreet make on Friday, and what did it change?
qa.a: He chose to tell Parul calmly how the rewriting affected him; they agreed on a Monday plan check and his own daily replies, and he answered forty messages alone.

qa.q: How might Parul see the Monday plan check compared with rewriting every post?
qa.a: Parul still gets to guide the page each week, which may ease her worry, while no longer carrying every single post herself.

grounding: Shows a teammate under constant correction feeling distrusted and stopping his own judgment, then naming the impact and agreeing on a clear check-in point.

passage: Mentor's note, fortnightly check-in. Avni, second year in the design team, seemed flat today. She said Urmila, her lead, now reviews every email before it goes out and asks for photos of her whiteboard sketches. "I've stopped deciding anything," Avni said. "I just wait to be told." I watched her pick at her nails. We practised one calm sentence: "When every step is checked, I stop trusting my own judgement. Can we agree on two check-ins a week instead?" This afternoon I saw her go into Urmila's cabin with a notebook. She came out twenty minutes later and said, "Tuesdays and Fridays." Next step: I will ask how the first week goes.

qa.q: What does Urmila ask for photos of?
qa.a: Avni's whiteboard sketches.

qa.q: How was Avni feeling about the constant checking?
qa.a: She felt flat and distrusted, so much that she had stopped deciding anything.

qa.q: What made Avni's talk with Urmila work?
qa.a: She named the impact calmly in one prepared sentence and proposed clear check-in points.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel hearing Avni's sentence?
qa.a: Urmila may feel surprised, then relieved to have a clear plan instead of checking everything.

grounding: Shows a young professional who feels distrusted under constant checking and restores balance by naming the impact calmly.

passage:
Thursday. Shankar texted me six times today about the plumber: what time he's coming, whether I asked for the bill, whether I checked the pipe myself. I've lived in houses with pipes my whole life. By evening I realised I'd stopped deciding anything at home without asking him first, even which vegetables to buy. When did that happen? After dinner I said, as calmly as I could, "When you check everything, I feel like you don't trust me, and I've started doubting myself." He went quiet, then said he gets scared things will go wrong. We agreed: one message when a big job is done, and small things are mine. Let's see.
Indu

qa.q: How many times did Shankar text about the plumber?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: How has Indu been feeling under all the checking?
qa.a: Indu feels distrusted and has started doubting personal judgement, even about vegetables.

qa.q: What did Indu do that helped restore balance?
qa.a: Named the impact calmly and agreed on one clear check-in for big jobs, with small things left to Indu.

qa.q: How does Shankar explain his checking?
qa.a: He says he gets scared things will go wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a partner under constant checking who stops trusting their own judgement, then names the impact and agrees check-ins.

passage:
At the dairy cooperative office in their small town, Harish checked Indu's milk-collection entries every hour. He redid her sums, rearranged her files and asked, "Did you call the Patil farm? Show me the call log."
By the third month, Indu had stopped deciding anything herself. When a farmer asked for a later collection time, she said, "Ask Harish sir." She went home tired and felt small.
One Friday, she waited until the office was empty. "Sir, can I say something? When every entry is checked, I feel you don't trust me. I've started doubting things I know how to do."
Harish blinked. "I just don't want errors."
"Neither do I. Could you check my register once, on Friday evenings? And I'll come to you for anything above the usual amount."
He was quiet. Then he nodded. "Let's try it for a month."

qa.q: How often did Harish check Indu's entries?
qa.a: Every hour.

qa.q: How did Indu feel after months of being checked?
qa.a: She felt distrusted, tired and small, and began doubting things she knew how to do.

qa.q: What did Indu do to restore balance?
qa.a: She calmly named the impact on her and proposed clear check-in points: a Friday review and coming to him for anything above the usual amount.

qa.q: How might Harish see his own checking?
qa.a: Harish sees it as preventing errors, not as distrust, which is why Indu's calm explanation surprised him.

grounding: Shows a colleague who stops using her own judgment under constant checking, then calmly names the impact and agrees clear check-in points.
